column1: # Hadith 3 — Islam is built on five (Ibn Rajab's commentary, batch 1)

column2: ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

“Islam has been built on five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger, establishing the prayer, paying the zakāh, pilgrimage to the House, and fasting Ramaḍān.”
Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

The two of them recorded this hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs in the narration of ʿIkrimah ibn Khālid from Ibn ʿUmar. Muslim also recorded it through two other routes from Ibn ʿUmar, and it has further routes from him.
This hadith has also been narrated by Jarīr ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Bajalī from the Prophet ﷺ; Imam Aḥmad recorded his hadith.
Islam was discussed in the preceding hadith.

What this hadith means is that Islam is built on these five: they are like the pillars and supports of its building. Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī recorded it in Kitāb al-Ṣalāh, and his wording is: “Islam has been built on five supports,” and he went on to mention it.

The point is to liken Islam to a building whose supports are these five. The building does not stand without them, and the rest of the traits of Islam are like the finishing of the building: if any of them is missing, the building is deficient but still standing, and does not collapse through that deficiency — unlike the collapse of these five supports,
for Islam undoubtedly disappears when all of them are lost, and it likewise disappears when the two testimonies are lost. By the two testimonies is meant faith in Allah and His Messenger.
In a narration that al-Bukhārī mentions without its chain:
“Islam has been built on five: faith in Allah and His Messenger…” and he mentioned the rest of the hadith.
In a version in Muslim: “on five: that Allah be worshipped as One”; and in another of his versions: “that Allah be worshipped and all besides Him be disbelieved in.”
From this it is known that faith in Allah and His Messenger is included within Islam, as was established in the previous hadith.
As for establishing the prayer, a number of hadiths have come showing that whoever abandons it has left Islam. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Jābir, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Between a man and shirk and disbelief is abandoning the prayer.” The like of it is reported from the hadith of Buraydah, Thawbān, Anas and others.

Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī recorded, from the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not abandon the prayer deliberately, for whoever abandons it deliberately has left the religion.”

In the hadith of Muʿādh, from the Prophet ﷺ: “The head of the matter is Islam, and its pillar is the prayer.” He made the prayer like the pole of a tent, without which the tent neither stands nor stays up: if the pole fell, the tent would fall, and it could not stay up without it.
ʿUmar said: There is no share in Islam for one who abandons the prayer. Saʿd and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: Whoever abandons it has disbelieved.
ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaqīq said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not consider the abandoning of any deed to be disbelief except the prayer.
Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said: Abandoning the prayer is disbelief; there is no disagreement about it.

A group of scholars of the Salaf and of later generations held this view. It is the view of Ibn al-Mubārak, Aḥmad and Isḥāq, and Isḥāq related the consensus of the people of knowledge on it. Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī said: It is the view of most of the hadith scholars.

A group of them held that whoever deliberately abandons any of the five pillars of Islam is a disbeliever by doing so. This is reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Nāfiʿ and al-Ḥakam; it is one of the reported positions of Aḥmad, chosen by a group of his followers, and it is the view of Ibn Ḥabīb among the Mālikīs.
Al-Dāraquṭnī and others recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, who said: It was said: O Messenger of Allah, is the Ḥajj every year?
He said: “If I said yes, it would become obligatory for you; if it became obligatory for you, you would not be able to do it; and if you abandoned it, you would disbelieve.”

Al-Lālakāʾī recorded, by way of Muʾammal, who said: Ḥammād ibn Zayd told us, from ʿAmr ibn Mālik al-Nukrī, from Abū al-Jawzāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās — and I can only think that he traced it back to the Prophet — who said:

“The handholds of Islam and the foundations of the religion are three, and on them Islam has been founded: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, the prayer, and the fast of Ramaḍān.

Whoever abandons one of them is a disbeliever by it, and his blood is lawful. You will find someone with much wealth who has not performed Ḥajj, and he remains a disbeliever by that, yet his blood is not lawful; and you will find someone with much wealth who does not pay zakāh, and he remains a disbeliever by that, yet his blood is not lawful.” Qutaybah ibn Saʿīd narrated it

from Ḥammād ibn Zayd as mawqūf (stopping short of the Prophet ﷺ) and abridged; and Saʿīd ibn Zayd, Ḥammād’s brother, narrated it from ʿAmr ibn Mālik with this chain as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ), and said:

“Whoever abandons one of them is a disbeliever in Allah; nothing is accepted from him, neither obligatory nor voluntary, and his blood and wealth have become lawful,” and he did not mention what comes after.
It is reported of ʿUmar that he imposed the jizyah on those who did not perform Ḥajj, saying: They are not Muslims.

And of Ibn Masʿūd, that whoever abandons zakāh is not a Muslim. There is also a reported position of Aḥmad that abandoning the prayer and zakāh specifically is disbelief, but not abandoning fasting and Ḥajj.
Ibn ʿUyaynah said: The Murjiʾah called the abandoning of obligations a sin on a par with committing forbidden acts, but the two are not the same,
for committing forbidden acts deliberately, without holding them lawful, is disobedience, whereas abandoning the obligations without ignorance or excuse is disbelief.
The explanation of this lies in the case of Iblīs, and of the Jewish scholars who acknowledged with their tongues that the Prophet ﷺ had been sent but did not act on his laws.
Aḥmad and Isḥāq cited the disbelief of Iblīs for not prostrating to Ādam as evidence that whoever abandons the prayer is a disbeliever; and failing to prostrate to Allah is graver still.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “When the son of Ādam recites a verse of prostration and prostrates,
Satan withdraws weeping and says: Woe is me! The son of Ādam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so Paradise is his; I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so the Fire is mine.”

Know that these five supports are bound up with one another, and it is reported that some of them are not accepted without the others, as in the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Ziyād ibn Nuʿaym al-Ḥaḍramī, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“There are four things that Allah has made obligatory in Islam; whoever does three of them, they will avail him nothing until he does them all: prayer, zakāh, the fast of Ramaḍān and pilgrimage to the House.” This is mursal; it has also been reported from Ziyād, from ʿUmārah ibn Ḥazm, from the Prophet ﷺ.

It is reported from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, from his father, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The religion is five things, none of which Allah accepts without the others: the testimony that there is no god but Allah

and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger, and faith in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, in Paradise and the Fire, and in life after death — this is one; the five prayers, the pillar of the religion, for Allah does not accept faith except with prayer; and zakāh, a purification from sins,

for Allah does not accept faith or prayer except with zakāh. Whoever does these and then, when Ramaḍān comes, deliberately abandons its fast, Allah will not accept from him his faith, his prayer or his zakāh. Whoever does these four and then has the means to perform Ḥajj,

but does not perform it, does not make a bequest for it, and none of his family performs it on his behalf, Allah will not accept from him the four before it.” Ibn Abī Ḥātim mentioned it, and said: I asked my father about it, and he said: This is a munkar (objectionable) hadith; possibly it is the words of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī.
I say: Apparently it is his explanation of the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, and ʿAṭāʾ was one of the eminent scholars of al-Shām.
Ibn Masʿūd said: Whoever does not pay zakāh has no prayer.

Denying acceptance here is not meant as denying validity, nor does it mean that the prayer must be repeated because of the failure [to pay zakāh]; what is meant is that Allah is not pleased with it, does not commend the one who does it or praise him for it in the highest assembly, and does not boast of him to the angels.
So whoever carries out these pillars properly attains acceptance in this sense, while whoever carries out some of them and not others does not attain it,
even though he is not punished for what he did carry out with the punishment of one who abandons it; rather, his obligation is discharged by it, and he may even be rewarded for it.

From this it is known that committing certain forbidden acts by which faith is diminished can prevent the acceptance of certain acts of obedience — even one of the pillars of Islam — in the sense we have mentioned, as the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Whoever drinks wine, Allah will not accept a prayer from him for forty days”; and he said: “Whoever goes to a diviner and believes what he says, no prayer of his will be accepted for forty days”; and he said: “Any slave who runs away from his masters, no prayer of his will be accepted.”

The hadith of Ibn ʿUmar is cited as evidence that when a name covers a number of things, the name does not necessarily disappear when some of them disappear. This refutes those who say that if deeds were included in faith, faith would have to disappear with the disappearance of any deed included in what it names;
for the Prophet ﷺ made these five the supports and the structure of Islam and explained Islam by them in the hadith of Jibrīl,
and in the hadith of Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbaydillāh, in which a Bedouin asked the Prophet ﷺ about Islam and he explained it to him with these five.
Yet those who oppose us on faith say: If one trait of Islam, or four traits apart from the two testimonies, were lost, he would not thereby leave Islam.

Some of them have related that Jibrīl (peace be upon him) asked the Prophet ﷺ about the laws of Islam, not about Islam; but this wording is not authentic according to the imams and critics of hadith, among them Abū Zurʿah al-Rāzī, Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj, Abū Jaʿfar al-ʿUqaylī and others.

Scholars have likened faith to a tree with a root, branches and boughs. The name “tree” covers all of that, and if any of its boughs and branches were lost, the name “tree” would not be removed from it; one would only say that it is a deficient tree, or that another is more complete than it.

Allah has struck this likeness for faith in His words, Exalted is He: “Allah has struck a parable: a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firm and whose branches are in the sky, yielding its fruit at every season by the leave of its Lord” [Ibrāhīm 14:24–25].
The word is the word of tawḥīd; its root is the tawḥīd firmly fixed in hearts; and its fruit is the righteous deeds that grow from it.

The Prophet ﷺ likened the believer and the Muslim to the date palm. If any of the palm’s branches or fruit were lost, the name “palm” would not be removed from it altogether, even though it is deficient in branches or fruit.
Jihād is not mentioned in this hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, even though jihād is the best of deeds. In one narration, Ibn ʿUmar was asked: What about jihād?
He said: Jihād is good, but this is how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ narrated it to us.
Imam Aḥmad recorded it.

In the hadith of Muʿādh ibn Jabal: “The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and the peak of its hump is jihād.” The peak of its hump is the highest thing in it, but it is not one of the supports and pillars on which it is built, for two reasons.
The first is that jihād is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah) according to the majority of scholars, not an individual one, unlike these pillars.
The second is that jihād will not continue to be carried out until the end of time. When ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) descends, and no religion then remains but Islam,

war will lay down its burdens and jihād will no longer be needed — unlike these pillars, which remain obligatory on the believers until the command of Allah comes while they are still upon them. Allah knows best.
